questions.stem: What is a transitional fossil?
options: A fossil that has been moved from one rock layer to another by earthquakes or erosion
A fossil of a species that lived for only a short time, used to date the rock layers
A fossil formed when an organism's soft tissue turned slowly into hard mineral crystals
A fossil with features of both an ancestral group and a later group descended from it
questions.explanation: Transitional fossils show intermediate combinations of features, such as fish-like and limb-like traits together, supporting gradual change between groups. A short-lived, widespread species used for dating is an index fossil.

questions.stem: Tiktaalik, a fossil about 375 million years old, had gills, scales and fins like a fish, but also a flattened head, a neck and fin bones resembling a wrist. Why is it important evidence for evolution?
options: It proves that modern fish are descended from early land-living tetrapod ancestors
It is an index fossil, showing that all fish lived at the same time in the past
It is a transitional form between fish and four-limbed land vertebrates (tetrapods)
It shows that fish and tetrapods appeared at exactly the same time with no ancestor
questions.explanation: Its mix of fish features and tetrapod features is what evolution predicts for an animal near the origin of limbed vertebrates. Tetrapods descended from fish-like ancestors, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Fossils of early whales such as Basilosaurus had tiny hind limbs that could not have supported walking. What does this suggest?
options: Whales are evolving hind legs and will be able to walk in the future
Whales and fish share a recent common ancestor that had no limbs at all
Whales grew hind legs during their lives by trying to walk on land
Whales evolved from land-dwelling ancestors with functional hind legs
questions.explanation: Reduced hind limbs with no clear function are best explained by descent from four-legged land mammals, with the limbs reduced over many generations. Other fossils show a sequence of increasingly aquatic forms.

questions.stem: Why is the fossil record incomplete, with relatively few transitional fossils found?
options: Transitional organisms never existed, because species appear suddenly in their present forms
Transitional fossils are destroyed by scientists who date them using radioactive methods
Only plants form fossils, so the evolution of animals cannot be traced in rocks at all
Fossilisation needs rare conditions, soft tissue seldom preserves, and many rocks are eroded
questions.explanation: Most organisms decay before they can be buried, soft-bodied organisms rarely fossilise, and many fossil-bearing rocks have been eroded, deeply buried or not yet searched. Many transitional fossils have nevertheless been found.

questions.stem: Which conditions most favour the formation of a fossil?
options: Being eaten by a predator, so that the remains are protected inside its digestive system
Rapid burial in fine sediment with little oxygen, ideally of an organism with hard parts
Slow decay on the ground surface in warm, moist air with plenty of oxygen and bacteria
Exposure to sunlight and wind on a rocky hill, where scavengers can reach the remains
questions.explanation: Quick burial protects remains from scavengers and decay, and low oxygen slows bacterial breakdown. Bones, shells and teeth are far more likely to be preserved than soft tissue.

questions.stem: Researchers searching for a fish-tetrapod transitional form deliberately looked in rocks of an age between the oldest known lobe-finned fish and the oldest known tetrapods, laid down in shallow streams. They found Tiktaalik. Why does this strengthen the theory of evolution?
options: The researchers dated the rocks using the fossil, so the fossil's age could not be in doubt
The theory made a testable prediction about where and in which rocks such a fossil would be found
The fossil was found by chance, which shows that transitional fossils can turn up in any rock layer
The fossil proved that tetrapods are older than fish, which reversed the predictions of the theory
questions.explanation: A strong theory makes predictions that could fail. Evolution predicted that intermediate forms should appear in rocks of a particular age and environment, and the prediction was confirmed.

questions.stem: What is a fossil assemblage?
options: A single fossil that has been reassembled from bones found at different sites
The sequence of rock layers at a site, from the oldest to the youngest
A collection of fossils of one species from many different continents
The group of different fossil species found together in the same rock layer
questions.explanation: An assemblage is the set of fossils preserved together, which shows the community of organisms living at one time and place. Comparing assemblages in successive layers shows how life changed.

questions.stem: Fossil assemblages in a cliff change from layer to layer: lower layers contain only marine invertebrates, middle layers add fish, and upper layers include land plants and amphibians. What does this sequence show?
options: The kinds of organisms living in the area changed over time
All of these organisms lived together at the same time
The oldest organisms were the land plants and amphibians
The rock layers were deposited in random order over time
questions.explanation: Lower layers are older, so the assemblages record a sequence of different communities, with new groups appearing over time. This matches the order of appearance predicted by evolution.

questions.stem: The Ediacara Hills in South Australia contain fossils of soft-bodied organisms more than 540 million years old, among the earliest known complex multicellular life. What does this assemblage show?
options: Complex multicellular organisms appeared only after mammals and flowering plants had already evolved
All modern animal groups had already evolved, with the same forms that they have today
Soft-bodied organisms always fossilise more easily than organisms with shells or bones
Complex multicellular life existed before the major spread of animals with shells and skeletons
questions.explanation: The Ediacaran fossils show diverse multicellular life in rocks older than those with abundant shelled animals, recording an early stage in the history of complex life. Soft bodies preserve only under unusual conditions.

questions.stem: Fossils of marine shellfish are found in rock layers in a hilly area far inland. What is the best explanation?
options: The shellfish evolved to live on land after the sea had moved away from them
Birds carried the shellfish inland and dropped them in the hills
The rocks formed on land and were then flooded by the sea later
The area was once covered by sea, and the rocks were later uplifted
questions.explanation: Marine fossils show the sediment was laid down under the sea; geological processes later raised the rocks above sea level. Fossils therefore provide evidence of past environments as well as past life.

questions.stem: A band of igneous rock cuts vertically through four layers of sedimentary rock. What can be concluded about its age?
options: It is the same age as the highest of the layers it cuts through
It is younger than all four of the layers that it cuts through
It is older than all four of the layers that it cuts through
It is the same age as the lowest of the layers it cuts through
questions.explanation: A rock body must already exist before something can cut through it, so the intrusion formed after all four layers were deposited. This is the principle of cross-cutting relationships used in relative dating.

questions.stem: At site 1, fossil species M occurs in a layer just below a layer containing species N. At site 2, 300 km away, M and N are found in the same order. Both are short-lived, widespread species. What can be concluded?
options: The two sites cannot be compared, because rocks can only be dated at a single site
The layers with M at the two sites are about the same age, and so are the layers with N
The layers at site 2 must be older, because they are further from the original source
Species N must have evolved from species M, because N is always found above M
questions.explanation: Short-lived, widespread species make good index fossils, so matching them allows layers at different sites to be correlated in age. Order in the rock alone does not prove that one species descended from the other.

questions.stem: In undisturbed rock, layer A is the lowest, then B, C and D on top. A fault cuts through A, B and C but not D. Fossil X occurs only in B. Which statement is correct?
options: Fossil X is older than layer D, and the fault formed after layer C but before layer D
Fossil X is younger than layer D, and the fault formed before layer A was deposited
Fossil X is older than layer A, and the fault formed after layer D was deposited
Fossil X is the same age as layer D, and the fault formed at the same time as layer B
questions.explanation: By superposition, B is older than C and D, so X predates D. The fault cuts C but not D, so it formed after C was laid down and before D covered it.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of relative dating?
options: It gives the ages of rocks in years, but not the order in which the layers formed
It works only on igneous rock, which very rarely contains any fossils
It works only on living organisms, so it cannot be used on fossils
It gives the order in which rocks and fossils formed, but not their ages in years
questions.explanation: Relative dating places events in sequence (older or younger) using superposition, index fossils and cross-cutting relationships. Absolute ages in years need radiometric dating.

questions.stem: Across the fossil record, the oldest rocks contain only simple single-celled organisms, while multicellular organisms appear in younger rocks. How does this support evolution?
options: It shows that simple organisms evolved from complex ones that later disappeared
It shows that all organisms appeared at once and then sank to different depths
It shows that single-celled organisms became extinct once multicellular life began
It fits the prediction that complex life evolved from simpler ancestors over time
questions.explanation: The order of appearance in rock layers matches the sequence expected if complex organisms descended from simpler ones. Single-celled organisms did not go extinct; they remain the most abundant life on Earth.

questions.stem: When comparing the DNA of different species, what does a greater similarity in base sequence indicate?
options: The species live in more similar environments today
The species have bodies that look more alike
The species have a larger number of chromosomes
The species shared a common ancestor more recently
questions.explanation: Mutations accumulate in separated lineages over time, so species that diverged recently have had less time to accumulate differences. Similar environments or appearance can arise through convergent evolution without close relationship.

questions.stem: Part of the same gene is sequenced in four species. W: ATGCCTGAATTCGGA. X: ATGCCTGATTTCGGA. Y: ATGCGTGATTACGCA. Z: TTGCGAGATTACGCC. Which species is most closely related to W?
options: Y and Z equally
Species X
Species Y
Species Z
questions.explanation: X differs from W at only 1 of the 15 positions, Y differs at 4 and Z at 7. The fewest differences indicate the most recent common ancestor with W.

questions.stem: In a protein of 100 amino acids, species P and Q differ at 3 positions, P and R at 15, and Q and R at 14. Which phylogenetic tree is best supported?
options: P and Q share a recent common ancestor, and R branched off earlier
P and R share a recent common ancestor, and Q branched off earlier
Q and R share a recent common ancestor, and P branched off earlier
All three branched from one ancestor at the same time, equally related
questions.explanation: P and Q are the most similar (3 differences), so they are each other's closest relatives. R differs from both by a similar, larger amount, so its lineage split off before P and Q separated.

questions.stem: Two species differ by 6% in the DNA sequence of a gene. If this gene's differences between two species accumulate at about 1% per 2 million years since they diverged, about how long ago did they share a common ancestor?
options: 12 million years ago
3 million years ago
6 million years ago
8 million years ago
questions.explanation: 6% ÷ 1% = 6 units of 2 million years, so 6 × 2 = 12 million years. Dividing 6 by 2 gives 3, which inverts the rate.

questions.stem: Which assumption must hold for DNA differences to be used as a molecular clock?
options: The gene is never affected by mutations in any of the species
The species being compared live in exactly the same habitat
Mutations in the gene accumulate at a roughly constant rate over time
Mutations in the gene happen only at times when the local environment changes
questions.explanation: A molecular clock converts the number of differences to time, which works only if changes build up at a fairly steady rate, calibrated using fossils of known age. A gene with no mutations would show no differences to measure.

questions.stem: In DNA hybridisation, single strands from two species are combined and heated. Hybrid DNA from species A and B separates at a higher temperature than hybrid DNA from species A and C. What does this show?
options: A and C have more matching bases, so they are more closely related than A and B
A and B have fewer matching bases, so they are more distantly related than A and C
Temperature affects only the hydrogen bonds in C, so no conclusion can be drawn
A and B have more matching bases, so they are more closely related than A and C
questions.explanation: More complementary base pairs mean more hydrogen bonds, so more heat is needed to separate the strands. A higher separation temperature indicates more similar sequences and a more recent common ancestor.

questions.stem: Two species of burrowing mammal look very alike, but their DNA sequences are very different, and each is genetically closest to a different, non-burrowing group. What is the best interpretation?
options: Their DNA must be wrong, because physical appearance is better evidence of relationship
They are closely related, and their DNA has changed because they live underground
They are the same species, because animals that look alike always share recent ancestors
Their similar appearance is due to convergent evolution, and they are not closely related
questions.explanation: Similar lifestyles can produce similar bodies in unrelated groups. DNA comparisons are less affected by such convergence, so they can reveal true relationships hidden by appearance.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree built from DNA data, species J and K are joined at a node, which is then joined to species L at a deeper node. Which statement is correct?
options: J evolved from K, which in turn evolved from L, the oldest living species shown on the tree
L is the common ancestor of J and K, and still lives alongside them today
J, K and L are equally related, because all three appear on the same tree
J and K share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with L
questions.explanation: Each node represents a common ancestor; the node joining J and K is more recent than the node joining them to L. Living species at the tips are not ancestors of one another.

questions.stem: What are homologous structures?
options: Structures sharing a basic plan inherited from a common ancestor, possibly with different uses
Structures with the same function in unrelated species, which evolved independently of each other
Structures that have lost their function over time but are still present in an organism
Structures that develop in an organism during its life in response to how it is used
questions.explanation: Homologous structures share an underlying plan because of common ancestry, even when used differently. Structures with similar functions but different origins are analogous, and reduced, functionless structures are vestigial.

questions.stem: The forelimbs of a kangaroo, a fruit bat and a dolphin all contain one upper arm bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones and five digits. What does this suggest?
options: They use their forelimbs for the same function, so the bones are arranged in the same way
They are the same species, because only one species can have the pentadactyl limb pattern
They inherited this pentadactyl limb from a common ancestor and modified it for different uses
They each evolved this limb independently because they all live in the same type of habitat
questions.explanation: The same bone pattern in limbs used for hopping support, flying and swimming is best explained by descent from a common ancestor, with natural selection modifying the limb in each lineage.

questions.stem: Some whales have small pelvic bones buried in their body wall, not attached to the spine. How are these explained by evolution?
options: They are new structures that whales are evolving to walk on land
They are homologous to the fins of fish and are used for steering
They are vestigial structures inherited from four-legged ancestors
They are analogous structures that evolved for swimming in fish
questions.explanation: Reduced bones with little or no function are vestigial: remnants of structures that were functional in ancestors. This matches the fossil evidence of whales evolving from land mammals.

questions.stem: Early embryos of fish, birds and humans all develop pharyngeal pouches near the throat. In fish these become gill structures, but in humans they form parts of the ear and throat. What does this indicate?
options: Vertebrates share a common ancestor, and development has been modified in different lineages
Human embryos breathe through gills for a short time before their lungs begin to work
Fish evolved from humans, keeping the gill structures that humans had already lost
Similar embryos show that all vertebrates live in water during their early development
questions.explanation: Similar early developmental stages, later diverging into different structures, are evidence of shared ancestry. Human embryos do not breathe through gills; the pouches develop into other structures.

questions.stem: A student argues that bird wings and bat wings show birds and bats are closely related. Which evaluation is best?
options: The wings are analogous flight surfaces that evolved separately, though both are modified forelimbs
The student is correct, because any two animals with wings must share a recent winged common ancestor
Bird and bat wings are vestigial structures, so they give no information about relationships
Wings are acquired characteristics that develop with use, so they are not evidence of evolution
questions.explanation: Both wings are modified tetrapod forelimbs, homologous as limbs, but flight evolved separately: birds fly on feathers, bats on skin stretched between long fingers. So wings as flight surfaces are analogous and do not show close relationship.

questions.stem: Fossils of the seed fern Glossopteris are found in Australia, South America, Africa, India and Antarctica. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Glossopteris was carried between the continents by early human travellers
These landmasses were once joined as Gondwana, and later drifted apart
Glossopteris seeds floated across thousands of kilometres of ocean
Glossopteris evolved separately on each continent from different ancestors
questions.explanation: Glossopteris had large seeds unlikely to cross oceans, so its wide distribution indicates the continents were joined when it lived. Biogeography links the distribution of organisms to the history of landmasses.

questions.stem: Most of Australia's native mammals, and almost all eucalypt species, are found naturally nowhere else. Which explanation does biogeography support?
options: These organisms arrived recently, carried from Asia by people within the last few centuries
Australia's long isolation as a continent let its lineages evolve separately from those elsewhere
Australia's climate is unlike any other, so these organisms were each created to suit it
These organisms evolved elsewhere and every population outside Australia has since died out
questions.explanation: After separating from the rest of Gondwana, Australia drifted in isolation for tens of millions of years, so its organisms evolved independently and many are endemic. Distribution reflects evolutionary and geological history.

questions.stem: Across a narrow deep-water channel in Indonesia (along Wallace's Line), the animals on the western islands resemble those of Asia while those to the east resemble those of Australia. What best explains this?
options: Animals on both sides evolved from the same recent ancestors only a few thousand years ago
Deep water kept the two regions separate for a long time, so their faunas evolved separately
The animals on each side were introduced by humans travelling between the two regions
The climate on each side is completely different, so the same animals cannot survive both
questions.explanation: Even when sea levels fell, the deep channels remained barriers, so the Asian and Australian faunas evolved in isolation. Wallace used this pattern as evidence that distribution reflects evolutionary history.

questions.stem: Species found only on an island often most closely resemble species on the nearest mainland, rather than species on islands with similar climates elsewhere. What does this suggest?
options: Island species evolved first and later colonised the nearest mainland from the island
Similar climates always produce identical species, wherever they occur in the world
The island species descended from mainland colonists and then diverged in isolation
Each island species was created to suit its island's climate and habitats exactly
questions.explanation: Colonists arrive from nearby land and then adapt to island conditions, so island species are related to mainland species. This pattern fits evolution, not separate origin to suit each climate.

questions.stem: Almost all living organisms use the same genetic code, in which the same codons specify the same amino acids. What does this suggest?
options: Every species evolved its own code that happens to be the same
Only closely related species share any genetic code at all
All life descended from a common ancestor that used this code
The genetic code changes to match each organism's environment
questions.explanation: A shared, essentially universal code is best explained by inheritance from a single common ancestor of all life. If life had arisen many times, many different codes would be expected.

questions.stem: Bacteria, plants and animals all use DNA, the same 20 amino acids in proteins and ATP as their energy carrier. Which evidence for evolution is this?
options: Anatomical evidence from homologous limbs
Biochemical evidence for common ancestry
Biogeographical evidence for continental drift
Fossil evidence from transitional forms
questions.explanation: Shared molecules and biochemical processes across all forms of life are biochemical evidence that they descend from a common ancestor. Biogeography concerns where organisms are found.

questions.stem: Why is the theory of evolution by natural selection regarded as strongly supported?
options: Independent lines of evidence from fossils, anatomy, biogeography and molecules all agree
A single complete fossil sequence shows every step in the evolution of every living species
Scientists have observed every major group of organisms evolving within a single human lifetime
Evolution has been proven true, so there is no longer any need to test it against new evidence
questions.explanation: Evidence from very different sources, gathered by different methods, points to the same relationships and sequence, which gives great confidence. Like all scientific theories, it remains open to testing.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of molecular evidence over fossil evidence when inferring relationships?
options: It gives absolute ages for rock layers without needing any radiometric dating
It can be used only for species that have left large numbers of fossils
It can be gathered from living species and gives numerical data that can be compared directly
It shows exactly what extinct species looked like and how their bodies were built
questions.explanation: DNA and protein sequences can be obtained from any living species and differences counted, making comparisons objective. Fossils, however, are the only direct evidence of extinct forms and their anatomy.
